https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: A billboard displays portraits of the deputy chair of the state Duma, Pyotr Tolstoy, and Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, promoting the United Russia party, Moscow, 15 September 2026. Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters View image in fullscreen A billboard displays portraits of the deputy chair of the state Duma, Pyotr Tolstoy, and Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, promoting the United Russia party, Moscow, 15 September 2026. Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters Opinion Russia To understand the threat to our real democracy, watch Putin’s fake one Rafael Behr As Russians vote this weekend, remember that Britain is not immune to the cynical tactics and corrosion of trust that keep him in power Wed 16 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.20 EDT Share M illions of people will participate in elections in Russia this weekend and a new parliament will be chosen, but not necessarily in that order. The purpose of the exercise is to maintain Vladimir Putin’s authority over the political process, which means United Russia, the president’s party, will retain control of the Duma. That much is settled before the polls open, although the scale of the government’s victory won’t be declared until the votes are counted. A portion of seats is available for other “systemic parties” that function as Kremlin licensed-opposition, padding out the pretence of pluralism. They serve as a pressure valves for public frustration and parliamentary proxies when rival factions within the ruling elite want to nudge Kremlin policy in one direction or another. The Kremlin likes to minimise the difference between United Russia’s official tally and a number that would plausibly reflect public attitudes to the regime. If the gap is too wide, achieved by fraud too blatant, it conveys insecurity in the Kremlin. Putin’s power doesn’t depend on endorsement by ordinary Russians but his authority is sustained by the illusion that he listens and cares. An egregiously stolen election would prove that he doesn’t. Everyone knows the result is fixed, but it would breach a social contract if the fiction became too absurd. Electoral verisimilitude is harder than usual to pull off this time because of war fatigue. No one can pretend any more that the “special military operation” in Ukraine has gone to plan. It was supposed to take weeks and is now in its fifth year. There have been about 1.5 million Russian casualties. A shortage of volunteers stirs fear that another mobilisation of unwilling army reserves is in the works. Putin has denied that any such draft is required. That he needs to offer public reassurance at all amounts to recognition that progress on the front has stalled and the mood at home has soured. Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have made the war visible and economically palpable thousands of miles away from the frontline. The veil of state propaganda cannot be drawn across plumes of smoke rising from oil refineries and queues at petrol pumps. There are no accurate opinion polls in an authoritarian state. Russians are disinclined to share their private thoughts with strangers on the phone, especially when denigrating the armed forces is a criminal offence. A more reliable indicator of growing dissent is the increased rate of its repression. Last month, Yabloko, an inconsequential liberal party, was barred from the elections on a preposterous trumped-up technicality. The real objection was the party’s campaign slogan – “For peace and freedom”. Yabloko had previously been tolerated as an irrelevant vintage party from the pre-Putin era, not exactly tame but unthreatening; not worth the risk of aggrandisement by political martyrdom. That calculus changed with signs that voters were drifting towards the only available anti-war banner. It wasn’t a big movement but enough to persuade the authorities that denying the party representation after the ballot could be messier than blocking it in advance. If banning the opposition depresses turnout, all the better. The Kremlin appears to have accepted that a sincere show of enthusiasm for the status quo is unavailable. A boring, low-key election, telling a story of submission and stability, is the next best thing. Such is the perverse craft of “managed democracy” – the mechanics of running gangster authoritarianism through a notionally liberal constitution. It requires a mix of performative coercion, tactical concession and confected consent. The economic spoils of corruption have to be dispensed widely enough to feed a quiescent elite. There has to be enough theatre of public participation to legitimise the regime. But genuine freedom must also be discredited as the path of chaos. That has been an easy line to sell to Russians who recall post-Soviet democratisation as a time of rampant gangsterism, surrendered superpower status and national immiseration. Putin is a product of that era and the embodied backlash against it. He transferred the engines of oligarchic capitalist self-enrichment to the reconstituted chassis of a Soviet-style state. He made himself an avatar for imperial nostalgia and an exhausted population’s craving for order. He promised to express the national interest more efficiently as its sole incarnation than any raucous, divided parliament ever could. That offer has less appeal in established democracies, where political pluralism and the rule of law have deeper roots, but it has an audience. The core proposition – a strong leader to avenge a once great country’s humiliation by foreigners – has twice carried Donald Trump to the White House. His ratings have plummeted but he can still count on credulous adulation from as many as one in three Americans. What is the equivalent number in Britain? The leading product in this market is Reform UK, which now polls around 23%, level with Labour. Nigel Farage’s position has slipped this year as his personal and party finances have come under scrutiny, but his core supporters are untroubled by the whiff of grubby lucre. For some, convinced that the whole system is a rotten sham, scandal around Reform UK’s receipt of multimillion-pound donations positively burnishes the brand. It proves that Farage is a baller, capable of beating the “establishment” parties at their own game – a gamble that the savvy, loadsamoney crypto crowd are backing. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion The deep cynicism feeding that judgment is a vital element in the chemical compound that corrodes democracy. I remember it as the most pungent feature of Russian politics when I lived in Moscow, watching the 90s experiment in democracy fail. It is the demoralised conviction that no politician would ever be motivated by a spirit of public service. The only categories are weak and strong; suckers and players. To succeed, a nation needs to be led by a strong player. Constitutions and laws are just parts of the toolkit for exercising power. The liberal view that holds them sacred as a system for holding governments to account is the mark of a sucker. Farage doesn’t put it quite like that. He did tell his party conference last week that an incoming Reform government would declare a “national emergency” to enact a radical agenda within the first 100 days and tolerate no objection from parliament, the courts or Whitehall. No one can say they weren’t warned. It isn’t an explicitly anti-democratic agenda but it never is with populists in opposition. No one wins elections by promising to cancel future ballots and, as the Russian experience demonstrates, once power has been secured, the well-managed poll is a valuable mechanism for consolidating control. There is a process of hollowing-out that comes first. It is a relentless corrosion of trust in independent institutions and the sluicing of public debate with caustic cynicism. It is the stirring of disillusionment and frustration into nihilistic rage against the system; sowing division and amplifying despair to make authoritarian rule sound like release from political paralysis. Russia was lost down that road long ago. British democracy is thankfully more robust, more culturally embedded. Or so we hope. Resilience is not immunity. The Putin model of venal cynicism that dresses authoritarian kleptocracy in a call for national redemption won’t declare its motives in an election campaign. The democratic fightback can’t wait until that election to see how far the poison has spread. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Trump has no legal right to demolish the Kennedy Center, which was established by Congress. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Trump has no legal right to demolish the Kennedy Center, which was established by Congress. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images Donald Trump Analysis Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Center has put its future at risk David Smith in Washington The president has threatened to block renovations and suggested the landmark could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename it Sat 19 Sep 2026 09.30 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 09.31 EDT Share It was born with the world premiere of Leonard Bernstein’s Mass. “Young people will come here and they will see this cultural centre,” Rose Kennedy, the mother of slain US president John F Kennedy, said at that opening night gala . “They will carry some of these ideas back to their different communities.” More than half a century later, the potential death knell came just after 4.30pm on Tuesday with a perfunctory announcement on the public address system: “The centre is now closed to the public. Please exit the centre by way of the Hall of States.” Soon barricades had been erected and security guards were blocking access. The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC, once filled with the buzz of audiences and children, had fallen as silent as a mausoleum. Now a high stakes legal battle is under way to prevent Donald Trump from taking a wrecking ball to the building that is both national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. The current White House occupant, incensed that courts have prevented his name being added to the Kennedy Center, told reporters this week: “I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down.” On social media, Trump declared the venue “destined to doom” without his intervention. View image in fullscreen Donald Trump looks down from the presidential box in the Opera House at the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts as he participates in a guided tour and leads a board meeting on 17 March 2025. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images The once unthinkable threat became more thinkable when an Agence France-Presse photographer took a picture of Trump aboard Air Force One, holding a placard with ominous red text: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame. Below was a big picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building. Trump has no legal right to demolish the facility, which was established by Congress. Critics say he is acting out of spite because he cannot get his way. Kerry Kennedy , the former president’s niece , said: “Like a child who can’t play with a toy, he wants to stomp on the toy. But this is not a toy. This is the living memorial to a slain president. “It would be like adding the Trump name to the Trump-Lincoln Memorial or the Trump-Jefferson Memorial or Trump-Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The courts have spoken, he cannot demolish it, he cannot put his name on it and he should be focused instead on his job. ” The Kennedy Center did not respond to requests for comment. The 100ft structure opened in 1971 on the banks of the Potomac River. Since then it has presented ballet, children’s theatre, comedy, contemporary dance, hip-hop, jazz, international festivals and educational programmes. The annual Kennedy Center Honors have hosted past presidents and a who’s who of US arts and culture. View image in fullscreen President John F Kennedy looks at a model of the Kennedy Center on 8 October 1963 in Washington DC. Photograph: National Archives/Getty Images Trump seized control of the facility in February 2025, claimed its finances were in dire straits and fired board members who did not align with his “vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture”. Deborah Rutter, the centre’s president, was ousted and replaced by Ric Grenell, a Trump loyalist and former ambassador with no experience in arts management. An initiative created in 2020 to promote anti-racism and community outreach was shut down and its 10-person staff dismissed. Citing “drag shows specifically targeting our youth”, any programming perceived as “woke” was purged. It was a commercial disaster as audiences, performers and philanthropists deserted the centre in droves. Lawyer Norm Eisen, who has litigated against the administration’s attempts to impinge on institutional independence, said: “He slapped his name on there and destroyed the lifeblood of the Kennedy Center: audience and artists.” In January, the Kennedy Center hosted the world premiere of Melania, a documentary about the first lady , with the Trumps in attendance. Three days later, the president announced that he would be closing the facility for two years for $257m repairs and renovations. View image in fullscreen Reflected in the Potomac River, the exterior of the John F Kennedy Center of the Performing Arts building is lit up in multiple colors in advance of the annual Kennedy Center Honors on 1 December 2024. Photograph: J David Ake/Getty Images The Trump-appointed board backed the move and also voted to rename the venue the “Trump-Kennedy Center”. Trump’s name was duly added to the exterior marble facade, before the US district judge Christopher Cooper intervened and ruled that only Congress has the authority to rename the memorial. The name was removed but the result remains hidden by giant scaffolding and tarpaulins. Asked about Trump’s motivations, Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action added: “You would need an authority in abnormal psychology to get the answer to that question but he appears to have developed an obsession because he’s not used to hearing the word no.” On Tuesday this week, Judge Cooper again ruled that the Trump administration could not put a new Trump sign on the Kennedy Center’s facade or rename its plaza for the president “without Congress’s blessing”. Hours later, the centre’s board voted to close the facility for two years, citing the need for $257m of repairs and renovations. The centre’s executive director, Matt Floca, ordered an immediate seven-day emergency closure, citing “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration”. But Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse allege that the closure is a “pretext” to hide a financial “death spiral” caused by artist boycotts and dwindling ticket sales. View image in fullscreen Construction workers build scaffolding near the sign for the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts on 12 June. Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images In an interview on Friday, Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment and public works committee and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board of trustees, said the events represented three phases of Trump’s assault on the complex. “One is what I call the mob bust out gone wrong, in which they tried to take over and run the Kennedy Center, give themselves and their friends big contracts , charge expensive goodies to Kennedy Center accounts, do political favours using Kennedy Center facilities for Trump allies, and that was extremely damaging to the business of the centre,” he said. “Then they moved into the renaming fiasco and that seems to have struck a lethal blow to the centre’s business model – a predictably damaging blow that they failed to consider at all. Now they’ve moved into a third stage in which they are threatening the actual destruction of the Kennedy Center if they don’t get their renaming.” Whitehouse added: “It has gone from bad to worse but the through line in all of this is that these trustees are under a legal duty to put the welfare of the centre itself first and, if they fail in that duty, they create a legal environment in which courts can and ultimately likely will step in to make sure that the centre is run lawfully.” The legal battle intensified on Thursday, when Judge Cooper issued an order requiring the Kennedy Center to give at least 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition. Whitehouse said: “There’s a contrast between the thuggery and bullying world in which you could countenance a threat to tear down the Kennedy Center if your name doesn’t go on it and the actual legal world in which actions have to be approved by a board that has a fiduciary duty to put the welfare of the institution first. Those two are irreconcilable at this point.” View image in fullscreen Donald Trump threatened to keep the Kennedy Center closed for good after a judge ruled his name cannot be added on to the famed arts institution’s facade on 15 September. Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images Still, Trump ordered the demolition of the White House East Wing to make way for a ballroom, despite opposition from preservationists and questions over the administration’s authority to proceed without Congress. He is now threatening to cancel the renovation of the Kennedy Center, and warning of its possible demise, if his name is not restored to the building. Chris Raleigh, an organiser the Hands Off the Arts movement, which is mobilising grassroots resistance, said: “That’s what you do when the hostage takers can’t get what they want. There comes a point where the hostage is inconvenient. Look at it: the people who have fought back have pushed Trump to the brink here. “In no way at all is he winning. His name is not going up on the building. There is somebody in the White House every day who says, before they walk in that building, ‘Oh god, please don’t let there be another Kennedy Center story today.’ ” Raleigh added: “Everyone in Trump’s life should be telling him: ‘You gotta to get out now. This is not going to help you.’” And even if the current peril passes, it will be difficult to restore the centre to its former glories. On Friday it laid off about a dozen staff, the Washington Post newspaper reported . Michael Kaiser , who led the centre from 2001 to 2014, warns that even a two-year closure will be damaging. He said: “When you don’t have audiences and you don’t have donors participating for two years, those individuals go elsewhere. When you have no staff, even if there’s a time in the future where we can return to a more sense of being normal, it’s not going to be so simple to reopen a building of this size and complexity.” Some critics see the attack on the Kennedy Center as part of a broader assault on institutions and freedom of expression. On Friday, Trump announced that the media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico would be banned from the White House and, with health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr standing behind him in the Oval Office, railed against the Kennedy Center again. To Kerry Kennedy, who has worked in the human rights arena for 45 years , the president is a “petty tyrant”. Asked to consider the possibility of the Kennedy Center being lost, she reflected: “It would be devastating for my family because we love Uncle Jack but in the end Trump is not going to hurt my family. He is hurting our country and he’s hurting our world and he’s giving permission to tyrants everywhere to shut down arts centres and silence critical voices.” On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins. The speakers included a drag queen. Against the setting sun, protesters beat drums and waved signs that read: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Our center not DJT’s”; and “Wicked starring DJT”. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8zx.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The comedian's supporters gathered outside the courthouse in Istanbul on Monday with signs that translate to "Deniz GÃ¶ktaÅ not alone" By Orla Guerin Senior international correspondent ,Â Reporting from in Istanbul Published 28 September 2026 An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan â and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months â but ordered his release due to time served. It has also placed him under a travel ban, preventing him from travelling outside Turkey. A final decision in the case will come from the court of appeals. Deniz GÃ¶ktaÅ - who denied the charges - has already spent nearly 90 days in prison. Prosecutors had asked for up to 12 years. His case comes amid a wave of arrests in Turkey that human rights groups say is aimed at crushing dissent. His stand-up routine went viral on YouTube, attracting more than 15 million views. Prosecutors had singled out a line in which the comedian called the Turkish leader "a shy dictator", but GÃ¶ktaÅ insisted there was "no criminal element" in his comments. "Dictator is not an insult," he said, "it is a political characterisation." But angering the president in Turkey is not funny. GÃ¶ktaÅ was arrested and handcuffed at Istanbul airport in July when he returned from a holiday. During his court appearance on Monday, it was clear he did not lose his sense of humour during his 88 days in solitary confinement. "Three months have been taken away from my life," he said on the stand. "But I quit smoking, so I'll add another three months to my life." That drew laughter and loud applause in court. Outside, supporters like Firat Aksal â a fellow comedian â were very pleasantly surprised by the verdict. "We hardly know what to do with our happiness," he said. "We are thrilled. To be honest we weren't hopeful of getting a fair trial. " GÃ¶ktaÅ was released at 21:45 local time (18:45 GMT) and greeted by well-wishers, including his parents who he was seen hugging, outside a prison facility. Aksal said GÃ¶ktaÅ would now rest for a few days, and see his family, and then return to the stage. After his release, GÃ¶ktaÅ told reporters: "I'm very happy to be reunited with my family, mother, father, and friends." But he added: "There are thousands of other people in prisons across Turkey. Some, like me, are being held in pre-trial detention, while others have been convicted because of their views. "So, of course, it's wonderful to be out. I've missed it very much. But there is not much difference between inside and outside. I hope the day comes when we can all regain our freedom together." Many others remain behind bars, including journalists, human rights campaigners, student protesters, LGBTQ activists, and the elected Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu. Prisons are full in Turkey these days. Erdogan and his party in the past have denied arrests, such as that of Imamoglu, have been politically motivated , insisting that Turkey's judiciary is independent. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Albertans take part in a pro-Canada Rally, at the provincial legislature ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Edmonton on 18 October. Photograph: Todd Korol/Reuters View image in fullscreen Albertans take part in a pro-Canada Rally, at the provincial legislature ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Edmonton on 18 October. Photograph: Todd Korol/Reuters Canada Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights ‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz says Leyland Cecco in Toronto Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico , she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F). “I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying. But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others. This week, Alberta held a referendum , asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms. While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed . “I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.” The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers. The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis. The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education. Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said : “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.” ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists Read more Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff. Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation. “I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare. Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically. “Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.” For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration , the government position has shifted. Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits. “Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.” The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services. But González argues that there is no data to back that claim. Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan. “In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.” She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed. “The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.” Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation. “This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.” During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US. For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province. “We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here.
